html:
The Suda is a huge Byzantine Greek encyclopedia of about 30,000 entries on the ancient Mediterranean world, compiled in the late 10th century. Its title was once taken for the name of an author, Suidas, but it probably comes from a Byzantine word for a fortress.

The entries are in a kind of alphabetical order. They cover words, people, places and events, from grammar and proverbs to the lives of writers, philosophers and emperors, on Christian and pagan topics alike. The unknown compilers worked mostly from earlier dictionaries, notes and summaries, such as the excerpts collected under Constantine VII.

Its value today is that many of those sources are lost. Much of what is known of the lives of ancient writers, from Sappho to Aristophanes, comes from the Suda. It shows the same urge as the Bibliotheca of Photios and the Macedonian Renaissance: to gather and keep the learning of the ancient world in Constantinople.
